claims.text: GeoDeploy pairs TypeSafe Jev's confidence-scored decisions with the Pulumi Automation API to place and scale Kubernetes across AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud.
TypeSafe AI opened early access to Jev, their SystemOne model, in the past week (relative to this post's 2026-09-25 publish date).

TypeSafe's Jev comes with a set of AI primitives (choice, score, noul) that let apps, agents, and workflows make decisions based on context, returning typed answers with calibrated confidence rather than free text.
GeoDeploy compares every AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud region that offers managed Kubernetes and provisions consistent environments across all three hyperscalers.
In GeoDeploy's design, the TypeScript app takes in the request, fetches live pricing, and does all the math, but never makes judgment calls.
In GeoDeploy's design, Jev decides which region wins and which modules to use, but never does arithmetic, generates code, or invents region names.
In GeoDeploy's design, Pulumi provisions clusters, registries, workloads, and DNS, but never decides anything.
In GeoDeploy's pipeline, each business region (geo) is mapped to a canonical location and residency class as the first pipeline step.
GeoDeploy enumerates every region with managed Kubernetes and uses great-circle distance as a coverage measure.
GeoDeploy fetches current prices from the AWS Price List API, the Azure Retail Prices API, and the Google Cloud Billing Catalog, normalized into a single quote format.
claims.source_hint: AWS Price List API / Azure Retail Prices API / Google Cloud Billing Catalog

claims.text: GeoDeploy's TypeScript logic deterministically bin-packs pods onto nodes, filters out instance types that don't match the image's architecture, and computes a monthly cost for each candidate region.

GeoDeploy assembles a Pulumi program from a curated registry of typed modules including EKS, AKS, or GKE; ECR, ACR, or Artifact Registry; ingress; DNS through Route 53, NS1, or Cloudflare; and observability.
The Pulumi Automation API runs a preview and then an update, with one stack per region, and will not run at all unless the user's cloud credentials pass readiness checks.
Every GeoDeploy run writes a plan.json and plan.md file with the full decision record, and a web UI shows the deployment on a live globe.
Jev's choice() primitive picks one option from a closed list and returns the pick, a probability distribution across all options, and a confidence score.
Jev's score() primitive rates something against a rubric the caller describes, and GeoDeploy uses 10 levels for its rubrics.
Jev's noul() primitive answers a yes/no question with a single probability.
Jev only ever selects from closed sets defined by GeoDeploy, choosing among region IDs that GeoDeploy has already priced and checked, and never writes code or does arithmetic.
For each geo, GeoDeploy sends Jev a shortlist of up to 40 priced candidates, along with the constraints and the image's architecture, in a single call.

In its single call to Jev, GeoDeploy requests a region selection, five quality scores (coverage, cost fit, maturity, sprawl risk, and architecture consistency), two hard checks (data residency and capacity), and a fallback region choice.
TypeSafe advises describing situations, not degrees, when writing rubrics for its scoring primitive.
The options passed to Jev's choice() function are the priced candidates themselves, keyed by ID, so Jev cannot answer with a region that isn't on the list.
GeoDeploy's five quality scores feed a ranking system with weight profiles: latency-optimized (the default), balanced, residency-first, and failure-domain.
Because GeoDeploy's ranking weights live in code rather than being decided by Jev, the ranking can be re-tuned without calling Jev again.
GeoDeploy's latency-optimized weight profile assigns weights of cost 0.13, coverage 0.48, maturity 0.17, sprawl 0.1, and archConsistency 0.12.
GeoDeploy's balanced weight profile assigns weights of cost 0.25, coverage 0.25, maturity 0.2, sprawl 0.12, and archConsistency 0.18.
GeoDeploy's residency-first weight profile assigns weights of cost 0.12, coverage 0.12, maturity 0.38, sprawl 0.23, and archConsistency 0.15.
GeoDeploy's failure-domain weight profile assigns weights of cost 0.08, coverage 0.17, maturity 0.48, sprawl 0.15, and archConsistency 0.12.
In GeoDeploy, cluster and registry modules follow directly from the provider (AWS always means EKS and ECR), leaving Jev to decide ingress posture, autoscaling posture, and node-pool sizing tier.
GeoDeploy checks every Jev answer against a confidence threshold matched to how risky the decision is, per a six-row table of decisions, thresholds, and fallback actions.
GeoDeploy's data-residency decision uses a confidence threshold of 0.95, below which the AI region selection is hard-rejected.
GeoDeploy's region-for-a-new-cluster decision uses a confidence threshold of 0.90, below which the top three candidates are flagged for a human to choose.
GeoDeploy's region-when-a-stack-already-exists decision uses a confidence threshold of 0.75, below which the existing region is kept.
GeoDeploy's ingress-or-autoscaling-module decision uses a confidence threshold of 0.85, below which the registry default is used.
GeoDeploy's node-pool-sizing-tier decision uses a confidence threshold of 0.60, below which the bin-packing result is used.
GeoDeploy applies a global floor confidence threshold of 0.50 for region pick, residency, or capacity decisions, below which the AI path is dropped for that geo.
GeoDeploy's residency check is a hard gate that never soft-fails a compliance constraint, even by falling back to the model's own pick, hard-rejecting below a 0.95 threshold.
Each AiPathAborted error in GeoDeploy carries the full attempt (state, questions, and answers), so even a rejected answer ends up in the audit trail.

If a gate check fails, the Jev API times out or returns an error, or the upstream can't be reached, GeoDeploy switches to a deterministic fallback that compares prices across providers while still enforcing the residency and constraint checks.
Running `geodeploy explain` shows why each region won.

When self-driving mode is enabled via `geodeploy monitor`, the agent periodically checks each deployment's CPU utilization and asks Jev one joint question across all regions with options no-change, scale-up:<geo>, scale-down:<geo>, or shift:<from>-><to>, plus a separate disruption-risk check.
In GeoDeploy's self-driving mode, code rather than Jev computes the actual node-count changes.
In GeoDeploy's self-driving mode, a resize is applied automatically above 0.85 confidence.
In GeoDeploy's self-driving mode, a resize is suggested for human approval between 0.70 and 0.85 confidence.
In GeoDeploy's self-driving mode, below 0.70 confidence GeoDeploy ignores Jev's pick and falls back to a deterministic per-region rule based on observed utilization.
CPU utilization alone is described as a poor autoscaling metric, usually paired with other signals such as median end-to-end request latency or error rates once a traffic baseline is established.
The GeoDeploy project's source code is hosted at https://github.com/pulumi/devx-geodeploy.
The Pulumi Automation API is documented at /docs/iac/automation-api/.
TypeSafe Jev is documented at https://docs.typesafe.ai/introduction.
The Pulumi Automation API is linked at /automation/ in this post.
